title: Design-Specific New Approach Methodology Using Air-Liquid Interface (ALI) for Toxicological Testing
content: Air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures of pulmonary cells, such as human bronchial epithelial cells (HBECs) are widely used to study airway biology, disease mechanisms, therapeutic interventions, and toxico-pharmacological properties of drugs. We hypothesized that differentiation-dependent temporal shifts in epithelial phenotype result in distinct windows of biological responsiveness, and that pathway-specific transcriptional signatures can be leveraged to identify optimal intervention time points within ALI cultures using design-specific New Approach Methodology (NAM). We conducted a targeted genetic screening of key markers involved in DNA damage responses and inflammatory pathways. In addition, we measured the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) as a proxy for tight junction formation. By analyzing the temporal expression profiles of these genes at multiple time points (Day 0, 7, 14, and 21), we identified biologically relevant differentiation stages for experimental interventions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time such a recommendation has been proposed for ALI studies for toxicological testing. We propose a data-driven strategy to determine the optimal experimental window based on pathway-specific gene expression. This novel approach may enhance the reproducibility and accuracy of airway disease modelling, toxicity and drug testing, ensuring that studies are conducted at the most functionally relevant stage of differentiation.
